vignette:
Amina was 35 and worked as a tutor, usually in the late afternoons and evenings, meeting students in a small room at a community learning center and sometimes taking sessions online from her apartment. The assault happened after she had stayed behind to lock up one night, when a man she had trusted access to the building raped her in the quiet corridor near the classrooms. What she remembers most clearly is not a full narrative she can tell from beginning to end, but flashes that arrive with the same terror she felt in the moment: the hard edge of the hallway, her own nausea, the sound of her breathing, and then the sense that the event is like something that happened to someone else, not to her. She has said more than once that she cannot seem to put the frightening event into words, and when she tries to speak about it the story breaks apart before it becomes language. Even now, if children start crying in the center where she tutors, or if a student looks uncertain and asks her to repeat a direction, she feels her stomach turn and her mind jumps back to the assault, not because the situations are the same, but because they carry the same helpless uncertainty and bodily alarm that have become linked to what happened.

In the months afterward, those moments of crying or uncertainty did more than upset her; they pushed her into a bleak certainty that she had been permanently changed for the worse. Amina came to believe that if she thought too directly about the rape, she would not be able to handle it, and that even the slightest upset could undo her. That belief made her wary of anything that might stir feeling or hope. She began to avoid situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful, declining invitations from her partner to go out after work and turning down small celebrations at the center when a student improved, because joy felt dangerous, as if it might leave her open to collapse. She also became careful about being reminded of the event by others; if someone mentioned the building, asked why she no longer stayed late, or tried to bring up “what happened,” she pulled away and changed the subject. Her self-talk narrowed around blame, and she found herself repeatedly blaming herself for what happened, replaying every choice she had made that evening as if it could explain why she had not prevented it.

The more Amina tried to keep the memory at a distance, the more it seemed to press in from the side. She would catch a phrase, a smell in the hallway, or the sound of a child crying in the center and suddenly feel that same terror return, vivid and immediate, as if her body knew before her mind could catch up. Because the memory felt alien, like it belonged to someone else rather than to her, she kept circling it in her head, trying to force it into a story she could master. Instead, the effort seemed to deepen the divide; the event remained wordless and frightening, and her repeated self-blame only made the memory feel more contaminated and true. After days spent avoiding anything that might remind her of it, she noticed that the triggers seemed to be everywhere: a crying child in the tutoring room, the uncertainty in a student’s face, the sudden wave of nausea in her own body. Those moments reinforced her belief that she had been permanently damaged, and that she could not tolerate even small disturbances, which made her pull back still further.

As weeks passed, Amina’s avoidance shaped her life in concrete ways. She stopped volunteering for evening sessions, arranged her tutoring schedule so she could leave before the center got loud, and kept her phone silenced when her partner suggested plans that might feel warm or hopeful. When the memory surfaced, she pushed it away, only to find that the next reminder felt sharper. When she blamed herself, she became more convinced that she was broken. When she felt broken, she watched for signs of trouble in the room around her, bracing for crying, uncertainty, or a wave of nausea, and those sensations in turn made the memory feel closer and more threatening. By the time she sought help, she was exhausted by the way her days had shrunk around what she could not bear to think or feel. She came to therapy not because she believed the assault had lost its power, but because she was frightened by how thoroughly it was organizing her life, and she hoped, despite everything, that she might learn how to face the memory without being overwhelmed by it.
